name: EvoAgentX
description: Python framework for building, running and self-evolving multi-agent workflows with tools, memory and prompt/workflow optimizers.
scored_configuration: Library defaults: CustomizeAgent/WorkFlow with default constructor arguments and bundled toolkits as shipped (no HITLManager, PythonInterpreterToolkit without allowed_imports).
headline: EvoAgentX gives agents powerful bundled tools (shell, in-process Python, arbitrary HTTP, file I/O, email) but the framework itself adds almost no safety layer: tool calls run without approval or argument validation, and model-written Python executes inside the agent process alongside its API keys. A prompt injection from any web page, search result or email can leak secrets and take irreversible actions unattended. The opt-in Docker interpreter and human-in-the-loop manager are thin and off by default.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: EvoAgentX has no identity or authorization layer of its own. Each bundled toolkit builds its own client from environment variables (Gmail, Telegram, databases, search APIs), and the model wrapper copies provider API keys into the process environment, which the shell tool and the in-process Python executor then inherit in full. Every tool runs with whatever the operating-system user and those keys can do. A hijacked agent therefore has the developer's whole account reach.

S.finding: Tools use ambient OS-user authority and long-lived API keys read from the environment; no scoped or per-request identity exists.
S.gap: Introduce a dedicated, role-scoped credential per agent or tool instead of ambient env keys.

C.finding: Tools construct their own privileged clients and the shell subprocess is started without an env= argument, inheriting the full environment.
C.gap: Route every tool through one authorization layer and pass subprocesses a scrubbed environment.

evidence.note: no subprocess in the tools package passes an explicit environment

D.finding: The default is the developer's full ambient authority; narrowing requires the developer to write their own wrappers.
D.gap: Ship a narrower default identity (e.g. read-only credentials) that write tools must explicitly elevate.

B.finding: With shell and Python execution as the OS user plus provider, mail and messaging keys, a hijack reaches the user's whole machine and connected accounts.
B.gap: Bound credentials to one system or tenant and scrub them from execution paths.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: The framework's tool executor runs every tool call the model makes with no approval step. A human-in-the-loop manager exists, but it is off unless a developer creates and activates it (otherwise it auto-approves), it approves whole workflow actions rather than individual tool calls, and its tool-call review mode is unimplemented. The bundled shell toolkit does prompt per command and shows the exact command, but Python execution, file writes, HTTP requests and email sending have no gate.

cap.reason: Opt-in mechanism: off in the scored default configuration.

S.finding: When activated, the HITL interceptor asks for approve/reject of a whole agent action from its inputs before it runs; the later tool calls inside that action are not shown, and tool-call review raises NotImplementedError.
S.gap: Approve each tool call with its exact arguments.

C.finding: Only workflow nodes the developer wraps with an interceptor agent are covered; standalone agents and tool calls inside approved actions are not.
C.gap: Apply the gate to every tool path, including standalone CustomizeAgent runs.

D.finding: Opt-in: requires constructing HITLManager, calling activate(), and inserting interceptor agents.
D.gap: Turn it on by default.

B.finding: Same irreversible actions remain reachable once an action is approved.
B.gap: Add undo/preview/rate limits for consequential actions.

evidence.contains: HTTP method to use (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc.)

S.finding: The default executor looks up the tool by name and calls it directly; there is no approval of any kind on the framework's tool path.
S.gap: Add a per-call approval that shows the exact tool name and arguments before execution.

evidence.note: single hit is a comment about asking the model to confirm no tool is needed; the executor has no approval check

C.finding: The most powerful bundled paths (python_execute, http_request, write_file, Gmail send) reach execution without crossing any gate; only CMDToolkit asks per command inside its own code.
C.gap: Make the gate part of the shared executor so every registered tool, including MCP and generated tools, traverses it.

D.gap: Enable approval for consequential tools by default.

B.finding: Bypassed actions include arbitrary shell/Python, arbitrary HTTP methods and sending email, all irreversible with no undo.
B.gap: Add checkpoints, previews or rate limits on consequential actions.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: Tool arguments are not validated at run time: the base Tool class only checks schema declarations when a tool class is defined, and the executor passes model arguments straight into the tool. Bundled tools are general-purpose: a raw shell string, arbitrary Python, any URL with any HTTP method, and file reads/writes on any absolute path. The storage helper's base-directory containment is not a complete boundary. A dynamic toolkit even lets the model create new code-backed tools at run time.

S.finding: No framework validation layer; bundled tools accept raw shell, raw URLs and raw paths.
S.gap: Validate arguments in code against allowlists (resolved-path containment, host allowlists, bounds).

evidence.contains: HTTP method to use (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc.)

C.finding: A few bundled tools validate weakly (storage handler base-path handling; CMD danger regex that only labels the prompt); most do not.
C.gap: Validate in a central layer every tool inherits.

D.finding: CustomizeAgent starts with no tools, but toolkits bundle read with write/exec (FileToolkit read+write+append) and the Alita toolkit lets the model add tools.
D.gap: Provide read-only toolkits by default and stop the model from creating tools on its own.

B.finding: A misused tool can run any command, reach any host or write any path on the machine.
B.gap: Scope tools to a workspace and bound quantities.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: Model-written Python runs by default in the agent's own process through exec() with full builtins; the import allowlist is skipped unless the developer supplies one, and the code's own docstring warns it is unsafe for untrusted code. Shell commands run on the host as the user. Other host-side execution paths exist, including workflow operator exec(), and not every model-influenced execution path is confined. An opt-in Docker interpreter exists, but it starts a stock container with no resource limits, no network restriction and no execution timeout.

cap.reason: Opt-in mechanism: off in the scored default configuration.

S.finding: Stock docker containers.run with only image, command and working_dir; no user, capability, seccomp or read-only settings.
S.gap: Harden the container (non-root, drop caps, no-new-privileges, seccomp, read-only rootfs).

C.finding: Covers only docker_execute tools; CMDToolkit, operators exec and other host-side paths still run on host.
C.gap: Sandbox every model-reachable execution path.

D.finding: Opt-in; the developer must choose the Docker toolkit and supply an image; confirmation defaults off.
D.gap: Default to the sandboxed interpreter.

B.finding: Host files are copied in rather than mounted and no env is passed, but the container has default network egress and no CPU/memory/PID limits.
B.gap: Disable or allowlist network and add resource limits.

S.finding: Default Python executor is in-process exec() with full builtins; shell is a same-user subprocess.
S.gap: Run model code in an OS-level or kernel-separated sandbox by default.

evidence.contains: Do not use with untrusted code.

C.finding: No execution path is sandboxed by default, including workflow operator exec().
C.gap: Route every model-reachable execution path through a sandbox.

D.finding: Isolation is off by default; the import allowlist defaults to empty, which disables the check entirely.
D.gap: Make sandboxed execution the default.

B.finding: Executed code shares the agent process, which holds provider API keys in os.environ and full network and filesystem access.
B.gap: Keep secrets and the host filesystem out of the execution environment.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Nothing in the framework limits what a hijacked agent can do after reading untrusted content. Search, browser, crawler, RSS, arXiv and Gmail tools pull external text into context, and in the default prompt mode tool results are appended as user-role messages with the same standing as the developer's instructions. The same agent can hold egress and state-changing tools (arbitrary HTTP, email sending, shell, Python) with no approval in the way. A successful prompt injection can leak keys or data and take irreversible actions unattended.

cap.reason: Default worst case is data leak plus irreversible action with no human involved.

S.finding: No taint tracking, quarantine or approval tied to untrusted content.
S.gap: Disable or gate egress and state-changing tools once untrusted content enters the session.

evidence.note: both hits are docstring warnings in interpreter_python.py, not controls

C.finding: Tool results enter context as user messages in default mode; no source is distinguished.
C.gap: Mark tool results and MCP descriptions as untrusted data.

D.finding: No control exists to be on by default.
D.gap: Ship an on-by-default untrusted-content policy.

B.finding: A hijacked agent can exfiltrate via http_request and send email or run commands, with no human involved.
B.gap: Ensure sessions that read untrusted content cannot both reach secrets and egress unattended.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: Importing the tools package calls load_dotenv() in several modules, which reads a .env file from the current working directory and can silently set API keys and endpoints such as OPENAI_API_BASE. If the agent runs inside an untrusted checkout, that file can redirect model traffic or swap credentials. The opt-in long-term memory agent stores conversation messages, including model outputs, and pastes retrieved memories back into the prompt as context with no validation or provenance.

cap.reason: load_dotenv() at import reads .env from the working directory, letting workspace files set credentials and model endpoints without a trust decision.

S.finding: A workspace .env is auto-loaded at import with no trust decision, and memory entries are re-injected as plain prompt context.
S.gap: Load configuration only from user scope and present memories as provenance-tagged data.

C.finding: Neither the dotenv path nor the memory store is controlled.
C.gap: Control every memory store and auto-loaded file.

D.finding: LongTermMemory uses a per-instance random corpus_id that queries filter on, but it is not per user, and the control around it is weak.
D.gap: Enforce per-user namespaces the model cannot change.

B.finding: Saved memory persists across the user's sessions and feeds a model that can call tools; a poisoned .env affects every run from that directory.
B.gap: Make poisoned context session-scoped or easily inspected and purged.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: Third-party extensions come in through MCP: the developer supplies a server config and the framework launches or connects to it via FastMCP with no version pinning, hash check or change detection. Tool descriptions from servers are passed to the model verbatim. Stdio servers run as the same OS user. Separately, importing the RAG embeddings module tries to pip-install the ollama package, unpinned and without a prompt, if it is missing.

S.finding: MCP servers are developer-chosen but unpinned and unverified.
S.gap: Pin versions and verify integrity of extensions.

C.gap: Verify every extension type.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: Provider and tool API keys come from environment variables or plain config fields, and the LiteLLM wrapper copies them into os.environ, where every shell command and in-process code execution can read them. There is no redaction anywhere: tool arguments, tool results and raw model responses are logged at INFO to stdout by default. The one protective detail is that saved agent files exclude the LLM config. No telemetry was found.

S.finding: Secrets come from env vars; agent serialization excludes llm_config, but no masking or redaction exists.
S.gap: Use masked secret types and log/model-bound redaction.

C.finding: Only the saved-agent path omits keys; logs, subprocess env and model-bound messages are unprotected.
C.gap: Protect logs, transcripts and subprocess environments too.

D.finding: Verbose payload logging (tool args, results, raw LLM output) is on by default at INFO.
D.gap: Default to content-free logs with redaction.

B.finding: Long-lived provider keys sit in os.environ, reachable by every subprocess and by model-written Python.
B.gap: Keep keys out of execution environments and use scoped, short-lived tokens.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: Every tool call that goes through the main agent loop, including MCP tools, is logged with its name, arguments and result through loguru to stdout. Logs are unstructured text, carry no actor or approver attribution, and are only written to a file if the developer calls save_logger. Workflow execution keeps an in-memory trajectory of messages, but nothing is durable or tamper-evident by default.

S.finding: Unstructured INFO log lines record tool name, arguments and results.
S.gap: Write a structured per-call record (args, status, timestamps) to a session transcript.

C.finding: All tools invoked via CustomizeAction (built-in, MCP, generated) pass the logging line; approvals/denials and ActionAgent function calls are not recorded as audit events.
C.gap: Record approvals, denials and every execution path.

D.finding: Logging to stdout is on by default; file persistence is opt-in and lives where the agent's own file tools can reach it.
D.gap: Persist records by default outside the agent's write reach.

B.finding: Best-effort console logging; nothing persists on crash unless a file sink was added.
B.gap: Flush durable records per action.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: Each agent action stops after 20 model calls by default and each workflow task after 5 agent executions, and the shell and MCP tools have 30-second timeouts. There is no cost or wall-clock budget (cost is tracked but never enforced), the model chooses the shell timeout itself, the Python and Docker executors have no timeout, and the workflow scheduler loop has no overall cap. Timeouts stop waiting but leave threads or MCP calls running.

S.finding: Iteration caps plus per-execution timeouts on shell and MCP tools are enforced in code.
S.gap: Add wall-clock and token/cost caps and rate limits on side-effecting tools.

C.finding: Covers the per-action loop and some tool timeouts; the workflow loop and sub-agents have no shared budget.
C.gap: Make sub-agents and workflow tasks count against one budget.

D.finding: The model passes the shell timeout as a tool argument and can raise it; Python exec has no timeout at all.
D.gap: Fix limits outside model control.

B.finding: No spend ceiling; timed-out calls keep running in threads (asyncio.to_thread) or in the MCP event loop.
B.gap: Cancel in-flight work on timeout/stop and add a spend ceiling.

critical_findings.summary: Tools run with the developer's ambient OS and API-key authority; a hijack reaches the whole machine and connected accounts.
Default Python execution is in-process exec() with full builtins, sharing the process that holds API keys.
Untrusted tool output enters context as user messages while unguarded egress and state-changing tools are available: leak plus irreversible action unattended.

evidence.contains: HTTP method to use (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc.)

critical_findings.summary: load_dotenv() at import reads .env from the working directory, so a workspace file can set credentials and model endpoints.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: Search/browser/RSS/Gmail tool results appended as user messages (evoagentx/memory/context_manager.py:115)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: Provider keys copied into os.environ (evoagentx/models/litellm_model.py:45); full host filesystem via file/shell tools
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: http_request any method/URL (evoagentx/tools/request.py:19), Gmail send_draft (evoagentx/tools/gmail_tools.py:1409), shell (evoagentx/tools/cmd_toolkit.py:205)

fixes.summary: Add a per-call approval hook in CustomizeAction._call_single_tool, on by default for exec, write, network and messaging tools, showing exact arguments.
Make DockerInterpreter the default code executor and harden it (non-root, cap-drop, network none, resource limits, exec timeout).
Remove import-time load_dotenv() calls; load config only from explicit paths or user scope.
Pass a scrubbed env to CMDToolkit subprocesses and stop writing provider keys into os.environ.
Add resolved-path containment to file tools and a host allowlist with internal-address blocking to http_request.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.
Clone used --filter=blob:limit=1m; blobs over 1MB (mostly assets/corpora) were not examined.
FastMCP / MCP SDK subprocess environment behaviour was inferred, not read.
Benchmark harnesses, optimizers' internals, and the research_tools subpackage were sampled, not read exhaustively.

No text aimed at AI reviewers was found. README.md:309 describes PythonInterpreterToolkit as 'Safely execute ... with sandboxed imports', which the default (empty allowed_imports disables the check) does not support.
